This report formally initiates a multi-year study designed to document key wildlife species of significance to Whitefish (Goodfish) Lake First Nation #128 (WLFN #128). The project is led by [Mother Earth Environmental Services](https://www.motherearthenvironmental.ca/) (MEES), 100% owned by and operated in WLFN #128. The focus encompasses major game species - such as white-tailed deer, mule deer, and moose - in addition to furbearers and predators, including cougar, lynx, black bear, wolf, and coyote. The primary objective is to assess the impacts of oil sands development, specifically the cumulative effects arising from well-pads, pipelines, and other linear disturbances on the presence and abundance of these species within WLFN #128’s preferred harvesting areas.

A critical knowledge gap exists regarding how industrial landscape alterations influence wildlife distribution and habitat use in relation to traditional harvesting. This community-based monitoring program is structured to address two central questions derived from a community conceptual model:

-   First, are areas of oil sands development causing changes to the presence and abundance of key wildlife species within the Nation’s harvesting locations, thereby affecting species availability?

-   Second, is the community’s capacity to harvest wildlife through hunting and trapping being impacted by the ongoing and escalating pressure (the cumulative effects) of this development?

This project will incorporate community-based scientific monitoring with the Indigenous Knowledge (IK) of WLFN #128. While the wildlife cameras give us a boots-on-the-ground glimpse of what is going on, Harvester and Elder knowledge also give us important insight. They provide a deeper understanding of animal behaviour and populations, such as identifying game movement trends and key areas of interest for camera placement, and interpreting animal behaviour and health through the images. By bridging these knowledges, it enables us to have data that is scientifically strong, guided by community values and interests. Our work directly fulfills the goals of the OSM program by empowering MEES and WLFN #128 with these knowledge tools to find.

By systematically gathering evidence on these points, this study will generate vital data to understand the links between industrial activity and wildlife availability. This work directly fulfills the mandate of the OSM program by empowering MEES and WLFN #128 with independent, place-based knowledge to inform stewardship, management, and advocacy for its lands and resources.

As of February 2026, MEES deployed a total of 40 cameras:

-   Phase I Cameras - In 2024, MEES deployed 20 cameras around the main WLFN #128 reservation region, WLFN #128’s primary region of interest where approximately 2,000 WLFN #128 community members reside. These 20 camera locations were selected by MEES based on key areas of interest by WLFN #128 community members.

-   Phase II Cameras - In 2025, MEES deployed an additional 20 cameras - in clusters of four - within a secondary region of interest immediately northeast of the main WLFN #128 reservation region within locations that are affected by oil & gas development. These 20 camera locations were selected by MEES based on key areas of interest by WLFN #128 community members.

MEES will be able to compare both areas using the camera data with the idea of noticing any trends and changes in wildlife behaviour and abundance. The opportunity is also provided for WLFN #128 community members to observe any wildlife changes and trends from a generational perspective.

# Camera Refresh and Image Processing

MEES refreshed the 18 of the 20 total Phase I Cameras initially deployed in 2024 around the main reservation region in November 2025:

-   Upon retrieval, MEES unfortunately discovered one of the 20 Phase I Cameras (Camera WFL128-11) to be missing, and was unable to be located. MEES plans on searching for this missing camera in early Spring 2026 as soon as the snow melts.

-   Upon retrieval, MEES unfortunately discovered one of the 20 Phase I Cameras (Camera WFL128-18) was inaccessible due to extremely deep snow cover, and was unable to be retrieved. MEES plans on retrieving images from this camera in early Spring 2026 as soon as the snow melts.

MEES uploaded the images retrieved from the 18 Phase I Cameras to the online platform [WildTrax](www.wildtrax.ca). WildTrax is an online platform developed by the [Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute](www.abmi.ca) (ABMI) for users of environmental sensors - such as remote cameras - to provide support with processing, organizing, and sharing data.

# Project Highlights

A major highlight of our project was the combination and integration of IK with western environmental science. At the beginning of our project, MEES environmental professionals consulted with WLFN #128 community members to gain insight on wildlife “hotspots” based on their held IK. As most WLFN #128 community members are unavailable to participate in engagement sessions due to work commitments, our team adapted to bring the engagement session to them at work. This direct community involvement helped WLFN #128 feel a sense of belonging and connection with our project, making our project more meaningful and grounded in lived experience. Generations of local IK and understanding were shared and utilized to thoughtfully plan our project within its first year of execution, and for subsequent years of future wildlife monitoring. Meaningful collaboration resulted in a successful project, increasing authenticity and a sense of reward.

The process of wildlife camera trapping is lengthy and includes long periods of waiting for data to be collected. One of the initial phases of camera deployment involving physical exertion - including trekking and bushwhacking through remote areas - is nearly directly opposite of one of the final phases of data collection involving mental stimulation - including uploading, tagging, and analyzing tens of thousands of images in WildTrax - in an attempt to correlate the phases and complete the annual project as a whole. After a full year of data collection, viewing the memory card from each camera was synonymous with opening a time capsule which captured all wildlife passing by over the past year.

The wide variety of wildlife species captured by the cameras was of much interest to the MEES team. Of particular interest was the capture of one singular white-tailed deer fawn (@fig-fawn), as this age of deer is not known to wander without a doe, with the exception of if the fawn is bedded down in hiding while the doe forages. Viewing this image was very rare and unexpected, showing the resilience of this white-tailed deer fawn as an individual, and hope for its survival. The captured image also demonstrated not only presence, but reproductive success contributing to healthy wildlife populations.

# Camera Locations

As of February 2026, MEES has deployed a total of 40 cameras:

-   Phase I Cameras - In 2024, MEES deployed 20 cameras around the main WLFN #128 reservation region, WLFN #128’s primary region of interest where approximately 2,000 WLFN #128 community members reside. These 20 camera locations were selected by MEES based on key areas of interest by WLFN #128 community members.

-   Phase II Cameras - In 2025, MEES deployed an additional 20 cameras - in clusters of four - within a secondary region of interest immediately northeast of the main WLFN #128 reservation region within locations that are affected by oil & gas development. These 20 camera locations were selected by MEES based on key areas of interest by WLFN #128 community members.

The map below is an interactive map that can be used to explore the locations of the 40 cameras in total deployed by MEES. Satellite imagery can be switched on and off using the button in the top left of the top. Each camera location can be clicked on to show the camera name, assigned treatment (road, pipeline, or reference), and when it was deployed and refreshed.

<br>

```{r}
#| label: map-camera-locations
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Camera data ranges
location_ranges <- df_od |>
  mutate(project_location = paste0(project, "_", location)) |>
  group_by(project_location) |>
  summarise(start_date = min(date), end_date = max(date), .groups = "drop") |>
  separate(project_location, into = c("project", "location"), sep = "_") 

# Camera locations to map
locations_for_map <- df_location_reports |>
  left_join(location_ranges, by = c("location", "project")) |>
  filter(!is.na(latitude)) |>
  mutate(study = "WLFN #128 Primary Region of Interest") |>
  mutate(longitude = ifelse(longitude > 0, longitude * -1, longitude))

# Define icons for each study
icons <- awesomeIcons(
  icon = "camera",
  iconColor = "black",
  library = "ion",
  markerColor = "blue"
)

buffer <- 0.075

htmltools::tags$div(
  style = "display: flex; justify-content: center;",
  
  leaflet(data = st_as_sf(locations_for_map, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326), width = "90%", height = "750px") |>
  addTiles() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite Imagery") |>
  fitBounds(
    lng1 = min(locations_for_map$longitude) - buffer,
    lat1 = min(locations_for_map$latitude) - buffer,
    lng2 = max(locations_for_map$longitude) + buffer,
    lat2 = max(locations_for_map$latitude) + buffer
  ) |>
  addFullscreenControl() |>
  addResetMapButton() |>
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomright", options = scaleBarOptions(imperial = FALSE)) |>
  addMiniMap(position = "bottomleft") |>
  addAwesomeMarkers(
    icon = icons,
    group = "Camera Locations",
    popup = paste(
      "<b>", "Location: ", "</b>", locations_for_map$location, "<br><br>",
      "<b>", "Study: ", "</b>", locations_for_map$study, "<br><br>",
      "<b>", "Deployed:", "</b>", locations_for_map$start_date, "<br><br>",
      "<b>", "Refreshed:", "</b>", locations_for_map$end_date, "<br><br>"
    )
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c("Satellite Imagery", "Camera Locations"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE),
    position = "topright"
  )
)
```

## Independent Detections Over Time

The number of images of each species can tell us part of the grand picture; however, just because there may be more images of one species doesn’t necessarily mean there are more of them in the area, they may have just happened to spend more time in front of the camera. With camera data, it’s important to track the number of ‘independent’ detections for each species, considered to be an image or collection of images for a visit from an animal or group of animals.

For each camera, a 30-minute time interval is used to separate detection events; that is, images captured within 30 minutes of each other count toward a single detection, and images with a gap of greater than 30 minutes between them count as multiple independent detections. Images that are captured of the same species over less than 30 minutes are assumed to be of the same individual or group of individuals.

You can explore the figures for each species using the tabs below. The x-axis (bottom) represents the camera deployment timeline, from November 2024 to November 2025. The y-axis (left) shows the number of detections captured, aggregated from all of the cameras from the project. Note that the y-axis (left) for each species may change depending on the number of detections captured.

```{r}
#| label: ind-detections
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| include: true
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

species <- sp_uni

file_names <- paste0("Independent Detections ", species, ".png")

figure_letters <- letters[1:length(species)]

cat("::: panel-tabset\n\n")

for (i in seq_along(species)) {
  title <- species[i]
  letter <- figure_letters[i]
  img_path <- here::here("Figures/WFL128", file_names[i])
  rel_path <- fs::path_rel(img_path, start = getwd())

  cat("### ", title, " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
  
  # Output raw HTML as a single string
  html <- glue::glue(
    '<div style="text-align: center;">
       <img src="{rel_path}" style="width:80%;">
       <figcaption style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 0.5em;">
         <strong>Figure 6{letter}.</strong> Independent detections of <strong>{title}</strong> across the study time period.
       </figcaption>
     </div>\n\n'
  )
  
  cat(html)
  
}

cat(":::\n")

```

<br>

-   **White-tailed deer** detections were primarily recorded during the summer months, with a noticeable decline during winter 2025, a low point in March and April of 2025, and then rebounding during the summer.
-   Due to hibernation, **Black Bear** were not detected during the winter, and began in May 2025.
-   **Moose** detections were sporadic, with some concentration during June and July of 2025.
-   **Coyote** were also most frequently detected earlier on in the study period, particularly around February-April 2025.
-   **Red Fox** were primarily detected during the beginning of the study period, with hardly any detections after May 2025. A similar pattern was observed for **Snowshoe Hare**.

### Temporal Activity Patterns

As camera traps capture photos continuously - 24-hours a day, every day - they are able to indicate when certain species are active. These analyses can provide insight into competition, predation, and co-existence.

In this section we present the temporal (diel) activity patterns for each of the 6 focal species from the WLFN #128 cameras. The x-axis (bottom) of each of the following plots represents the 24-hr daily cycle, and the line represents the relative activity level detected by the cameras. This data is pooled across all the cameras deployed by WLFN #128.

```{r}
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: asis

# Set folder containing the plots
file_names <- paste0("Activity ", species, ".png")
figure_letters <- letters[1:length(species)]

cat("::: panel-tabset\n\n")

for (i in seq_along(species)) {
  title <- species[i]
  letter <- figure_letters[i]
  img_path <- here::here("Figures/WFL128", file_names[i])
  rel_path <- fs::path_rel(img_path, start = getwd())
  
  cat("### ", title, " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
    
    # Render the image and caption
  html <- glue::glue(
    '<div style="text-align: center;">
       <img src="{rel_path}" style="width:80%;">
       <figcaption style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 0.5em;">
         <strong>Figure 7{letter}.</strong> Daily activity pattern of <strong>{title}</strong> based on camera trap detections.
       </figcaption>
     </div>\n\n'
  )
  
  cat(html)
    
  }

cat(":::\n")


```

<br>

-   **White-tailed deer** displayed several activity peaks throughout the day, the most prominent of which were during twilight hours, specifically at dawn (6:00 to 9:00) and dusk (18:00). This pattern is known as *crepuscular*.
-   **Black Bear** showed a spike in activity near midday (12:00), with some smaller peaks later in the day.
-   Similar to White-tailed Deer, **Moose** demonstrated a crepuscular activity pattern, with peaks in the dawn (and later into the morning), as well as dusk after 18:00.
-   **Red Fox** were primarily noctural, with the most activity occurring during the nighttime.
-   **Coyote** were consistently active throughout the day, rising a little bit in the dawn after 18:00.
-   **Snowshoe Hare** activity increased throughout the evening beginning at 18:00, carrying throughout the night until dawn. They were not active during the day.

### Species Overlap

Blue colours indicate positive correlation, as two species are usually seen by the same cameras and share the same space. For example, Black Bears and Moose often appear in the same areas as they rely on the same habitat, such as forests which provide them both with food and shelter. Even though Black Bears sometimes hunt Moose - particularly calves - most adult Moose are large enough in size to defend themselves, meaning they don’t necessarily need to avoid Black Bear territory. Black Bears can also follow Moose for scavenging opportunities, which may keep them both in the same general area without constant conflict.

Red colours indicate negative correlation, as high counts of one species are usually accompanied with low counts of another species - and vice versa - as certain species tend to stay apart and are not usually seen at the same camera. For example, White-Tailed Deer may avoid areas with certain predators to reduce risk.

However, not all predators trigger avoidance; White-Tailed Deer and Gray Wolves may demonstrate a positive correlation, as White-Tailed Deer can be relatively fast and can rely on the same habitats as Gray Wolves. Gray Wolves are not able to catch every White-Tailed Deer, so White-Tailed Deer may tolerate the risk to access food or water.

### Species Density

We can use the number of images and counts of independent detections to estimate the density of each species at each camera. Density is the number of animals per unit area, which we express below as the number of animals per square kilometer (km<sup>2</sup>).

To estimate the density of each wildlife species at each camera, we used the Time in Front of Camera (TIFC) approach (@becker2022applying). This method has previously been used to estimate densities of unmarked populations of both White-tailed Deer and Moose in the boreal region of Alberta (@laurent2021evaluating, @dickie2024habitat). Similar to quadrat sampling, this approach involves (for each camera) multiplying the number of animals observed by the total time they spend in front of the camera, which is then divided by the product of the area sampled by the camera and the total time the camera was operating. This calculation yields an estimate of animals per unit area (i.e., 'density').

The following map displays the spatial distribution in densities of the 6 focal species between the cameras of the `r com_acr` camera wildlife monitoring projects. Note that cameras with no detections of a particular species (i.e., a density of '0') are represented with a black circle. Smaller circles represent small densities of a species at that camera. Bigger circles indicate that the density is higher at that camera.

<br>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" style="background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 5px;"}
You can hover over each camera location to see the calculated density of each species at that deployment, as well as use the 'Satellite Imagery' checkbox to turn on satellite imagery.
:::

```{r}
#| label: map-species-density
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

species <- c("Moose", "White-tailed Deer",
             "Black Bear", "Coyote", "Snowshoe Hare")

densities_to_map <- locations_for_map |>
  left_join(df_density_sum) |>
  select(-project) |>
  mutate(density_km2 = ifelse(density_km2 > 3, 3, density_km2)) |>
  mutate(log_density = log10(density_km2 + 1))

buffer <- 0.03

# Create base map
leaf_map <- leaflet(width = "95%", height = "550px") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", group = "Gray Canvas") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite Imagery") |>
  fitBounds(
    lng1 = min(densities_to_map$longitude) - buffer,
    lat1 = min(densities_to_map$latitude) - buffer,
    lng2 = max(densities_to_map$longitude) + buffer,
    lat2 = max(densities_to_map$latitude) + buffer
  ) |>
  addFullscreenControl() |>
  addResetMapButton()

max_log <- max(densities_to_map$log_density, na.rm = TRUE)

# Loop over species and add circle markers for each base group
for (sp in species) {
  
  data <- densities_to_map |>
  filter(species_common_name == sp) |>
  mutate(
    scaled_radius = pmax(log_density / max_log * 15, 4),
    fill_color = ifelse(density_km2 == 0, "#222222", species_colours[[sp]]),
    label_text = ifelse(
      density_km2 == 0,
      paste0(
        "<table>",
        "<tr><td>Camera location:</td><td align='right'><b>", location, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td colspan='2'><i>No detections at this location</i></td></tr>",
        "</table>"
      ),
      paste0(
        "<table>",
        "<tr><td>Camera location:</td><td align='right'><b>", location, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td>", species_common_name, " Density:</td><td align='right'><b>",
        round(density_km2, 2), " per km²</b></td></tr>",
        "</table>"
      )
    )
  )
  
  leaf_map <- leaf_map |>
    addCircleMarkers(
      data = data,
      lng = ~longitude,
      lat = ~latitude,
      radius = ~scaled_radius,
      fillColor = ~fill_color,
      fillOpacity = 0.85,
      stroke = TRUE,
      color = "#FFFFFF",
      weight = 1,
      group = sp,
      label = ~ lapply(label_text, HTML),
      labelOptions = labelOptions(
        html = TRUE,
        direction = "top",
        textsize = "14px",
        style = list(
          "padding" = "6px"
        )
      )
    )
}

leaf_map <- leaf_map |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = species,
    overlayGroups = "Satellite Imagery",
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE),
    position = "topright"
  ) |>
  hideGroup("Satellite Imagery")

tags$div(
  style = "display: flex; justify-content: center;",
  leaf_map)

```

# Where We Expect to Find Species

The ABMI compiles remote camera data collected in Alberta’s boreal region (including the Oil Sands Region) and uses it to develop habitat models for many species. These models incorporate species’ responses to land cover (e.g., vegetation and forest types), human disturbance, and climate variables (seasonal weather patterns).

The maps below show where the models predict each species is most likely to be found in the `r com_acr` area of interest. The area is divided into 1 km<sup>2</sup> pixels, and for each pixel, the model estimates the probability of each species being there based on the habitat and disturbance present in that pixel.

<br>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" style="background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 5px;"}
Use the buttons on the top right of the map to toggle through each species' predictions. You can also turn on **Satellite Imagery** and use the **NONE (Blank)** button to view the imagery underneath the predictions, as well as use the **Camera Locations** button to see where `r com_acr` camera locations are.
:::

```{r}
#| label: map-species-predictions
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

species <- c("Moose", "White-tailed Deer", "Red Fox",
             "Black Bear", "Coyote", "Snowshoe Hare")

# Load AOI
aoi <- st_read(paste0(g_drive_cbme, "WFL128/AOI/WLFN_Camera_AOI.shp"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Load rasters for each species
raster_list <- species |>
  set_names() |>
  map(~ terra::rast(paste0(g_drive_cbme, "WFL128/Predictions/", .x, " WFL128.tif")))

raster_list_clamped <- map(raster_list, ~ terra::clamp(.x, lower = 0, upper = 0.70, values = TRUE))

domain_raw <- c(0, 0.701)

pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "skyblue", "gold", "red"))(100),
  domain = domain_raw,
  na.color = "transparent"
)

#buffer <- 0.1

# Start building the leaflet map
map <- leaflet(width = "90%", height = "750px") |>
  addMapPane(name = "Basemap", zIndex = 410) |>
  addMapPane(name = "Satellite Imagery", zIndex = 420) |>
  addMapPane(name = "Species Rasters", zIndex = 430) |>
  addMapPane(name = "AOI Boundary", zIndex = 440) |>
  #addMapPane(name = "Camera Locations", zIndex = 450) |>
  addTiles(group = "Basemap", options = tileOptions(opacity = 1, pane = "Basemap")) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite Imagery", options = leafletOptions(pane = "Satellite Imagery")) |>
  addFullscreenControl() |>
  addResetMapButton() |>
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomright", options = scaleBarOptions(imperial = FALSE)) |>
  addMiniMap(position = "bottomright") |>
  addPolylines(data = aoi, color = "#0a0909", weight = 2, smoothFactor = 0.2, opacity = 1.0, fill = FALSE, options = leafletOptions(pane = "AOI Boundary"))

for (sp in species) {
  map <- map |>
    addRasterImage(
      raster_list_clamped[[sp]],
      colors = pal,
      opacity = 0.8,
      group = sp,
      options = leafletOptions(pane = "Species Rasters")
    ) 
}

map <- map |>
  addTiles(group = "NONE (Blank)", options = tileOptions(opacity = 0)) |>
  addAwesomeMarkers(data = st_as_sf(locations_for_map, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326),
                    icon = makeAwesomeIcon(icon = "camera", iconColor = "black", library = "ion", markerColor = "white"),
      group = "Camera Locations",
      popup = paste(
        "<b>", "Location: ", "</b>", locations_for_map$location, "<br><br>",
        "<b>", "Study:", "</b>", locations_for_map$study, "<br><br>",
        "<b>", "Deployed:", "</b>", locations_for_map$start_date, "<br><br>",
        "<b>", "Refreshed:", "</b>", locations_for_map$end_date, "<br><br>")) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = domain_raw,
    opacity = 1,
    title = "Probability of<br>Species Presence:",
    position = "bottomright",
    labFormat = labelFormat(
      transform = function(x) x * 100,
      digits = 0,
      suffix = "%"
    )
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c("Satellite Imagery",
                      "Camera Locations"),
    baseGroups = c(species, "NONE (Blank)"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  ) |>
  hideGroup(c("Satellite Imagery", "Camera Locations"))

# Print map

htmltools::tags$div(
  style = "display: flex; justify-content: center;",
  map)

```

<br>

-   **Moose** are expected to most abundant in the forested region of the area of interest.
-   **Red Fox** are relatively uncommon throughout the region of interest, but slightly more common in the south where agriculture is more prevalent.
-   **White-tailed Deer** are common throughout the region.
-   **Black Bear** are most common to the west of the region of interest, in the more forested areas.
-   Like Fox, **Coyote** are expected to be more prevalent in the south of the region in areas dominated by agriculture.
-   There is a small pocket of high quality **Snowshoe Hare** habitat in the west of the region, which is heavily forested.
